newsitem.title: SRI LANKA: Sri Lanka troops in build-up after fierce fight.
newsitem.headline: Sri Lanka troops in build-up after fierce fight.

text.p: Sri Lankan troops are fortifying northern areas captured from Tamil Tiger guerrillas last week before moving deeper into the rebel-held Wanni region, military officials in the north said on Tuesday.

They said there was an exchange of mortar and artillery fire overnight between the troops and the Liberation Tigers of Tamil Eelam (LTTE) rebels in the Omanthai area near Vavuniya, 220 km (135 miles) north of the capital Colombo, but no major clashes were reported.
"Bunkers will have to be built, supplies moved up, and the military needs to completely secure the area before moving ahead," one military official said.
A Defence Ministry spokesman said in Colombo that details were still awaited from the war front.

The LTTE said in an overnight statement the government was dramatically exaggerating rebel losses, and that only 60 fighters had been killed while the military's casualties had been carefully concealed.

The Defence Ministry said on Monday that rebel transmissions intercepted by the troops indicated that 181 rebels had been killed and 316 wounded in the offensive. It said the dead included several rebel leaders.

Troops backed by tanks, artillery and air cover broke out of their bases in northern Vavuniya and northeastern Welioya last week as part of an operation codenamed "Jaya Sikuru", or "Sure of Victory", in a bid to open a supply route to Jaffna peninsula, 100 km (60 miles) further north.
The rebels have accused the military of killing Tamil civilians and destroying property under the pretext of opening a supply route.
Journalists have not been allowed in the battle zone.

Troops on the offensive wrested control of Omanthai, 14 km (nine miles) north of Vavuniya, and northeastern Nedunkeni, about 40 km (25 miles) northeast of Vavuniya in the Wanni region, after fierce fighting last week.

The LTTE, fighting an ethnic war for an independent homeland for minority Tamils in predominantly Sinhalese Sri Lanka's north and east, control vast swathes of land in the mostly shrub-covered Wanni region.
The government says more than 50,000 people have been killed in the war. The LTTE say the number is higher.

Two divisions of the army, backed by the air force, were moving in two separate flanks in what military analysts and diplomats say is an attempt to cut across the LTTE-held areas to ensure that the rebels are spread thinly on the ground and unable to launch a concerted attack on security forces.
"The aim seems to be to dilute the power of LTTE by making them fight on two fronts and also prevent them from launching major attacks on the troops," one Asian diplomat told Reuters.

A military analyst said the military had broken LTTE forces into three parts by cutting across the Wanni region, which will make it difficult for the rebels to regroup quickly and launch major attacks. But he did not rule out surprise strikes on the troops.
But Tamil politicians have warned that although a major thrust would weaken the LTTE militarily, it could drive them away from the negotiating table.

"The LTTE is not likely to talk from a position of weakness. They will not come for negotiations under these circumstances," said Veerasingham Anandasangari, vice president of the Tamil United Liberation Front.
